title: AI Is Becoming a Member of the American Family — Ready or Not
excerpt: From homework help to meal planning, artificial intelligence has embedded itself in US households — but parents and children are divided on whether that's progress or dependency.
body:
• Nearly 9 in 10 American children ages 9–17 now use or interact with AI, with a quarter doing so daily, according to a Common Sense Media survey of 1,204 kids.
  • Deloitte's 2026 Back-to-School Survey found 49% of parents worry their child relies on AI too much, yet only 33% of schools have guidelines for its use.
  • Just 3% of US households pay for an AI subscription, but 64% of parents with kids under 18 want AI "family plans" bundled with streaming services.
  • A quarter of children say they turn to AI for homework help before asking a teacher or parent, raising concerns about dependency.

Artificial intelligence has moved from Silicon Valley buzzword to kitchen-table fixture in American homes. A national survey released in June by Common Sense Media found that nearly 9 in 10 children ages 9 to 17 now use or interact with AI tools — for entertainment, schoolwork, image generation, and advice on health and personal problems. About one in four use AI daily.

The speed of adoption has outpaced the rules meant to govern it. Deloitte's 2026 Back-to-School Survey, which polled 1,207 parents of K-12 students, found that 28% already use generative AI in schoolwork. Yet only 33% of schools have formal guidelines, and just 22% provide or recommend approved AI tools. Most striking: 38% of parents don't even know whether their child's school has an AI policy.

The Homework Battle

Nearly a quarter of children told Common Sense Media researchers they would turn to AI for help with homework before seeking guidance from a teacher, counselor, or parent. Students who struggled with math or essay writing were the most likely to lean on AI weekly or more.

"You can exploit AI to do all your assignments from school, and use multiple AIs to make it look handmade."

— Student respondent, Common Sense Media survey

One in five children who use AI said it would be difficult to stop for a month — rising to 42% among daily users. About one in ten agreed that AI "understands them better than most people do," with lonelier children more likely to use chatbots for emotional support.

Half of parents share that unease. Deloitte found 49% worry their child relies on AI too much, while 35% say schools aren't doing enough to prepare students for an AI-driven future. Some are responding on their own: 13% plan to pay for AI-related classes or tutoring outside school.

From Curiosity to Household Utility

Parents are warming to AI in their own way. A Qlik consumer survey found that 64% of parents with children under 18 want AI "family plans" — shared subscriptions with parental controls and a single bill, modeled after streaming services. Sixty percent said they were likely to invest within 12 months.

Yet actual spending tells a different story. Only about 3% of US households were paying for an AI subscription as of February 2026, according to the Bank of America Institute — though 10% more households paid up compared to the previous year.

"If you think back to Netflix and streaming services, at the beginning the growth was quite slow. Once that status quo is created, subscriptions will definitely start to go up sharply."

— Sekoul Krastev, co-founder, The Decision Lab

The Generation Gap

Even as AI becomes ubiquitous in young lives, enthusiasm among Gen Z is fading. A 2026 Gallup survey of more than 1,500 Americans aged 14 to 29 found excitement about AI fell 14 points in a single year, to just 22%. Anger jumped nine points to 31%. Nearly half of children surveyed had not discussed AI safety with a parent or teacher.

What It Means for Diaspora Families

For Indian-American households, where academic achievement is a cultural priority and many parents work in tech, the tension is especially pointed. Parents who use AI professionally now face the question of how much to let their children use it at home — without clear school-level guidance to lean on.

What Comes Next

OpenAI, which counts about 50 million subscribers, envisions the next phase as agentic AI — tools that act autonomously to plan vacations, manage shopping, and improve lives in the background. Nick Turley, head of ChatGPT, told NPR the company will likely always offer a free version but acknowledged that advanced AI assistants may remain behind a paywall. For now, AI's role in the American family remains a work in progress: adopted faster than it's understood, used more widely than it's governed.
